core: Working definition of inflammation (body's protective response to injury or infection; MedlinePlus/NCI-attributed)
The five classic signs: redness, heat, swelling, pain, loss of function (one line each + why each happens)
What inflammation does: contains damage, summons immune cells (phagocytes), starts repair; pus as the battle's end-product
Acute vs chronic inflammation with original examples (paper cut healing in days vs years of joint pain)
The immune connection: chemicals from damaged cells (histamine, bradykinin, prostaglandins) widen vessels and recruit white cells; fever as a systemic sign
Honest note: chronic inflammation can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs and contributes to disease
The 'inflammation is a fire alarm, not the fire' framing
supporting: Vascular mechanism behind each sign (widened vessels → redness/heat; leaky vessels → swelling; pressure + sensitized nerves → pain)
Fever as a sign of the body fighting illness or infection, not a disease itself
Inflammation vs infection distinction (a sprain inflames with no germ involved)
outOfScope: Wound-healing stages and tissue repair specifics (healing depth belongs to wound-care topics)
Anti-inflammatory drug mechanisms and dosing (pharmacology topics)
Specific disease diagnoses and treatment plans

claims.claim: Inflammation occurs when tissues are injured by bacteria, trauma, toxins, heat, or any other cause; damaged cells release chemicals (including histamine, bradykinin, and prostaglandins) that widen and loosen blood vessels, and the vessels leak fluid into the tissue causing swelling.

Inflammation is the body's protective response in which released chemicals trigger an immune response to fight off infection or heal damaged tissue; once the injury or infection is healed, the inflammatory process ends.
Phagocytes move into the inflamed area and engulf germs, foreign matter, and dead tissue; pus forms as a mixture of dead tissue, dead bacteria, and dead white blood cells.

The classic signs of inflammation are redness, heat, swelling, pain, and loss of function; redness and heat trace to widened vessels carrying more blood, swelling to leaky vessels letting fluid escape, pain to swelling pressure and sensitized nerves, and loss of function to the injured part not moving or working easily.
Acute inflammation begins quickly and ends when the injury or infection heals; chronic inflammation lingers for months or years and can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs.
Chronic inflammation can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs, and long-standing inflammation contributes to disease.

A fever is a body temperature higher than normal and is usually a sign that the body is trying to fight an illness or infection, not a disease itself; higher temperatures make it harder for many bacteria and viruses to survive.
Inflammation is the immune system's early response: the chemicals released by damaged cells both change the blood vessels and recruit the white blood cells that destroy invaders.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Inflammation is described as protective by the authoritative sources, yet the same sources document that it can be harmful when it persists — a framing tension the lesson must hold honestly.
positions: MedlinePlus and the NCI dictionary describe inflammation as the body's protective response that ends once injury or infection heals.
The NCI dictionary also states that chronic inflammation can damage healthy cells, tissues, and organs.
The lesson brief's honest-note requirement: chronic inflammation contributes to disease, stated factually without scare content.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches both sides in sequence: the protective purpose first, then a factual section on chronic inflammation's role in disease, held together by the 'inflammation is a fire alarm, not the fire' framing. No claim of causality stronger than the sources support ('contributes to' and 'can damage').

conflictingEvidence.issue: The number of classic signs varies across sources — the four classically attributed signs (redness, heat, swelling, pain) versus the five-sign list that adds loss of function.
positions: Older formulations name four cardinal signs.
The OpenStax Medical-Surgical Nursing text and this lesson's brief use five signs, adding loss of function.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses the five-sign list from the brief and the OpenStax text and does not claim the list is exhaustive; each sign is explained by its mechanism so the list is learned as logic, not memorized as trivia.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The machine-generated draft contained only boilerplate ('Inflammation is a foundational concept in Nursing & Allied Health Foundations...') with no substantive factual claims; nothing from it was carried into the lesson.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the machine-generated boilerplate draft with an original, source-verified lesson.
Anchored the working definition to MedlinePlus's encyclopedia entry (tissue injury by bacteria, trauma, toxins, heat, or any other cause) and the mechanism to the NCI Dictionary of Cancer Terms.
